card_quote: Likes debunking content online; argues in group chats. / Buying: low budget; borrows, uses library or e-book; buys print mainly as gifts for family.
how_read: Dipped in rather than reading in order. Did Round 1 to see if it was any good, jumped to Round 3 and 4 because that is psych and stats, skimmed Round 2, then read Round 5 in order. Stopped there because of exam season. Would take it to quiz night but hasn't opened rounds 6 to 10.

w1_friction.note: Tick boxes for sure or guessing. Feels like a worksheet, but ok for quiz night.
w1_friction.quote: tick whether you are sure or guessing.

w1_friction.quote: There is an apple in Newton’s own account

w1_friction.note: Everyone in physics knows the Nobel was for the photoelectric effect.
w1_friction.quote: Relativity is not what the prize named.

w1_friction.note: Why is there a Latin proverb in a Churchill answer? Dragged.
w1_friction.quote: everything that comes in threes is perfect

w1_friction.note: Stamp says TRUE, text says he never flew the kite. Also the number 31 is used twice. Typo or a draft page?

Same Wald story as the page before. Two entries to say armor where the holes aren't.
w1_friction.quote: The story is so neat that it is easy to doubt.

w1_friction.note: Another Laffer page straight after the napkin one. Padding.

w1_friction.note: Nobody thinks two researchers stand behind it. The 'popular version' here is made up so the answer can be TRUE.
w1_friction.quote: it is easy to suppose that two researchers stand behind the effect

w1_best.why: I was taught Stanford prison in intro psych with no critique. This is the one I'd bring up in the group chat tonight.
Milgram's 65 percent is only one condition, and nobody told me that. Good for an argument.
The Dunning-Kruger chart being a statistical artifact, and then a 2026 reanalysis flipping it. Real stats content.
Marshmallow test mostly explained by family background. I'd heard it was weaker but not why.
Monty Hall with the ten thousand letters and the hundred doors trick. I could explain it to my dad.

w1_flat.why: The second Newton apple page. One was enough.
The second Wald page, a repeat of the one before.
A second Laffer entry. I don't care about the Laffer curve once, let alone twice.
Churchill and 'blood, sweat and tears'. Nobody is going to fight over toil.
Baader-Meinhof. The answer is just 'it's named after a group', not much of a story.

w1_review.headline: Good for killing ten minutes before quiz night, but padded
w1_review.body: The psych and stats rounds are the best part, and the guess-then-turn format is fun with friends. It repeats itself, with two pages on Newton, Wald, Dunning-Kruger and Laffer, and one page (the Franklin kite) says TRUE while the text says the opposite. Bottom line: borrow it from the library, and maybe buy a copy for my dad.

w2_review_first: Honestly it's decent. I'd tell my roommate that the psychology experiments chapter is the best bit, and that you can read a story in two minutes and then argue about it. I wouldn't pay much for it though, and I'd tell him some stories show up twice.

w2_lost.why: Wald again. I'd already got it from the page before.
The Laffer napkin and then Laffer again. My eyes glazed over.
The Einstein Nobel one, because I knew it already.

w2_read_aloud.why: The 38 witnesses is the one everybody has heard, and the real story is a good gotcha.
People think Asch means most people cave. Two thirds held firm. Easy surprise.
The failed first camp is a nice twist that the textbook skipped.
Nobody knows who Little Albert was. That's a good unsettling one to read out.
The forgetting curve is based on one guy. People are always quoting it, so it lands.

w2_cut.why: Einstein's Nobel, known to anyone who did physics.

w2_book2: If it's priced above what I'd pay for an e-book, or if it's the same format with more repeated stories.
